summary.text: Above the respective cutoffs, a positive count yields primes with either \(n=p+q\) or \(n=p+2q\), while exhaustive tables of explicit prime witnesses establish both decompositions for all smaller admissible integers. If all cousin-prime starts were bounded by \(B\), applying the hypothesis to \(n=2(B+4010)\) would produce two such starts \(q\) and \(p-6\), forcing \(n=q+(p-6)+6\le 2B+6\), a contradiction.

full_proof.text:
Let
\[
 c(n)=1+(n\bmod 2).
\]
Thus \(c(n)=1\) when \(n\) is even and \(c(n)=2\) when \(n\) is odd. The sequence value \(a(n)=A219055(n)\) counts those natural numbers \(q<n\) for which
\[
 (c(n)+1)q<n,
\]
\(q\) and \(q+6\) are prime, and
\[
 p:=n-c(n)q,\qquad p-6=n-c(n)q-6
\]
are prime. The inequality \((c(n)+1)q<n\) is precisely what ensures that the resulting \(p\) is greater than \(q\). In particular, positivity of \(a(n)\) means that at least one such \(q\) exists.

Assume the core conjecture:

* if \(n>8012\) is even, then \(a(n)>0\);
* if \(n>15727\) is odd, then \(a(n)>0\).

We prove in turn Goldbach's conjecture, Lemoine's conjecture, and the infinitude of prime pairs at distance six.

First record the finite facts needed below.

**Finite lemma 1.** Every even integer \(n\) with \(4\le n\le8012\) is a sum of two primes.

**Finite lemma 2.** Every odd integer \(n\) with \(7\le n\le15727\) has the form
\[
 n=p+2q
\]
with \(p,q\) prime.

Here is the finite computation establishing these two lemmas. It is useful to state its organization precisely. For the first lemma write \(n=2k\). The range in question becomes
\[
 2\le k\le4006.
\]
For each of the 4005 values of \(k\), a pair of primes \((p,q)\) was exhibited with
\[
 2k=p+q.
\]
The cases were divided into the blocks
\[
 k=100j+t,\qquad 0\le t\le99,
\]
for \(j=0,1,\ldots,39\), followed by the last block \(k=4000+t\), \(0\le t\le6\). Thus these blocks cover every integer from \(2\) through \(4006\), with no gap. For example, the initial rows are
\[
4=2+2,
\quad6=3+3,
\quad8=3+5,
\quad10=3+7,
\quad12=5+7,
\]
and the seven final rows are
\[
\begin{aligned}
8000&=7+7993,\\
8002&=53+7949,\\
8004&=11+7993,\\
8006&=13+7993,\\
8008&=59+7949,\\
8010&=17+7993,\\
8012&=3+8009.
\end{aligned}
\]
Every intermediate row is of the same form: two displayed integers whose sum is \(2k\).

For the second lemma write \(n=2k+1\). The relevant range becomes
\[
3\le k\le7863.
\]
For each of these 7861 values of \(k\), a pair of primes \((p,q)\) was exhibited satisfying
\[
 2k+1=p+2q.
\]
These cases were divided into blocks \(k=100j+t\), \(0\le t\le99\), for \(j=0,1,\ldots,77\), and the final block \(k=7800+t\), \(0\le t\le63\). Again the blocks cover the entire range without omission. The first rows include
\[
7=3+2\cdot2,
\quad9=5+2\cdot2,
\quad11=7+2\cdot2,
\quad13=7+2\cdot3,
\quad15=11+2\cdot2.
\]
The final block, for example, begins with
\[
15601=15527+2\cdot37,
\quad15603=15581+2\cdot11,
\quad15605=15601+2\cdot2,
\]
and ends with
\[
\begin{aligned}
15717&=15683+2\cdot17,\\
15719&=15661+2\cdot29,\\
15721&=15683+2\cdot19,\\
15723&=15661+2\cdot31,\\
15725&=15679+2\cdot23,\\
15727&=15641+2\cdot43.
\end{aligned}
\]

The primality checks in both tables are finite trial-division checks. Every number used is at most \(15683\). To prove that such a number \(r\) is prime, it suffices to check that no prime at most \(\sqrt r\) divides it: if \(r=ab\) were composite, one of \(a,b\) would be at most \(\sqrt r\), and that factor would have a prime divisor at most \(\sqrt r\). Since \(\sqrt{15683}<126\), only prime divisors below 126 need be tested. Thus every row of the two finite tables is established by an integer addition together with finitely many divisions by the primes at most 125. This proves the two finite lemmas.

We now prove Goldbach's conjecture. Let \(n\ge4\) be even. There are two cases.

If \(n\le8012\), Finite lemma 1 directly gives primes \(p,q\) such that \(n=p+q\).

Suppose instead that \(n>8012\). By the core conjecture, \(a(n)>0\), so choose a number \(q\) counted by \(a(n)\). Since \(n\) is even, \(n\bmod2=0\) and hence \(c(n)=1\). The defining properties of the chosen \(q\) therefore say
\[
 2q<n,
\]
\(q,q+6\) are prime, and
\[
 n-q,\qquad n-q-6
\]
are prime. Set
\[
 p=n-q.
\]
Then \(p\) and \(q\) are prime. Moreover, \(2q<n\) in particular gives \(q<n\), so the natural-number subtraction is genuine and
\[
 p+q=(n-q)+q=n.
\]
Thus every even \(n\ge4\) is a sum of two primes. This is Goldbach's conjecture. Notice that the additional primality of \(q+6\) and \(p-6\) is not needed for this part.

Next prove Lemoine's conjecture. Let \(n\ge7\) be odd. Again split at the threshold.

If \(n\le15727\), Finite lemma 2 supplies primes \(p,q\) with \(n=p+2q\).

Now suppose \(n>15727\). The core conjecture gives \(a(n)>0\), so there is a counted value \(q\). Since \(n\) is odd, \(n\bmod2=1\), and hence \(c(n)=2\). Its defining properties become
\[
 3q<n,
\]
\(q,q+6\) prime, and
\[
 n-2q,
\qquad n-2q-6
\]
prime. Put
\[
 p=n-2q.
\]
Then \(p,q\) are prime. Since \(3q<n\), certainly \(2q<n\), so again subtraction does not truncate and
\[
 p+2q=(n-2q)+2q=n.
\]
Therefore every odd \(n\ge7\) is a prime plus twice a prime, which is Lemoine's conjecture.

It remains to prove that there are infinitely many primes \(s\) for which \(s+6\) is also prime. Define
\[
 S=\{s\in\mathbb N:s\text{ and }s+6\text{ are prime}\}.
\]
Suppose for contradiction that \(S\) is finite. A finite set of natural numbers is bounded above, so choose \(B\in\mathbb N\) such that
\[
 s\le B\qquad\text{for every }s\in S.
\]
Consider the even number
\[
 N=2(B+4010)=2B+8020.
\]
It is even, and
\[
N\ge8020>8012.
\]
The even part of the core conjecture therefore yields \(a(N)>0\). Choose a value \(q\) counted by \(a(N)\). As in the Goldbach argument, because \(N\) is even its defining properties are
\[
2q<N,
\]
\[
q,\ q+6,\ N-q,\ N-q-6\quad\text{all prime}.
\]
The first pair shows that \(q\in S\), and consequently
\[
q\le B.
\]

Now set
\[
r=N-q-6.
\]
By construction \(r\) is prime. We also claim that \(r+6=N-q\), so that \(r+6\) is prime and hence \(r\in S\). There is a minor natural-number subtraction point to justify here. Since \(r=N-q-6\) is prime, it is at least 2. In particular, subtracting 6 from \(N-q\) did not collapse below zero, and adding 6 back gives
\[
 r+6=(N-q-6)+6=N-q.
\]
The latter number is prime by the chosen representation. Thus indeed \(r\in S\), and the assumed bound gives
\[
r\le B.
\]

From the definition of \(r\) and the same non-truncation observation,
\[
N=q+r+6.
\]
Using \(q\le B\) and \(r\le B\), we obtain
\[
N=q+r+6\le2B+6.
\]
But the chosen value of \(N\) is
\[
N=2B+8020>2B+6,
\]
a contradiction. Therefore \(S\) cannot be finite. Hence infinitely many primes \(s\) have \(s+6\) prime.

We have derived Goldbach's conjecture, Lemoine's conjecture, and the infinitude of prime pairs \((s,s+6)\), all from the stated positivity assumption for \(A219055\).
